title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (n=300 task pairs) that measured whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, relative to direct LLM generation. The preregistration froze a single shared initial candidate per task (one generator call shared by both arms) and allowed a bounded guarded policy that performs at most one automatic repair call for the guarded arm when the shared initial fails. Under the declared generator snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) and the supplied 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest, every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator: baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred, the preregistered single‑repair policy was not invoked. We release the full preregistration, task manifest, model configuration, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts with canonical SHA‑256 hashes to enable exact reproduction and controlled follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models that translate operator intent into vendor CLI changes are increasingly proposed to speed NetOps workflows. However, operational trust requires that generated configurations satisfy safety invariants before being applied. A common operational architecture is generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R): a generator proposes a candidate configuration, a deterministic validator checks syntactic, resource and workflow invariants, and an automatic repair step attempts bounded fixes when the validator fails. Prior work argues for tool‑assisted self‑correction loops and verifier‑anchored guardrails to improve reliability (e.g., recent tool‑augmented self‑refinement work). Yet, evidence quantifying the marginal benefit of a bounded repair step—given a fixed generator and validator—remains limited. We therefore preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory experiment to estimate the paired improvement in validator pass probability yielded by allowing a single automatic repair call when the same initial candidate fails.

Research question. Under a shared‑initial paired design (one generator call per task shared by both arms), does allowing a single automatic repair call in the guarded arm increase the per‑task probability of producing a deterministic‑validator‑passing configuration compared to direct generation (the baseline)?

Contributions. (1) A machine‑readable preregistration freezing the experimental design and analysis (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6). (2) A curated 300‑task multi‑vendor intent manifest, a conservative deterministic validator, and an execution bundle containing all raw responses and provider traces (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). (3) A preregistered paired analysis executed exactly as specified: n = 300 pairs, exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CI (10k resamples, seed = 1729). (4) Full archival of artifacts and hashes enabling exact replay and controlled perturbations.
sections.related_work: Intent‑to‑configuration systems and LLM‑assisted NetOps have proliferated: recent intent‑based translation prototypes and NetOps benchmarks study translation and validation but rarely isolate bounded repair effects under a frozen experimental design. Representative verified references that motivated our design include: Nguyen et al. (Intent translation with LLMs; verified DOI 10.1002/nem.2313), Chakraborty et al. (CNSM 2024 NetOps automation work; verified proceedings note), and tool‑augmented self‑refinement pipelines (INTERACSPARQL; LATCH). Deterministic, SMT‑style verification systems for network policies (Bagpipe / Weitz et al., 2016) informed our validator construction and conservative scoring rules. We used the primary sources wherever available and recorded machine‑readable verification of each cited record (see Cited Record Ids). Our approach differs by preregistering a paired shared‑initial design that isolates the incremental utility of a bounded automatic repair call on the very same generator output.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline in machine‑readable form (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; SHA‑256 above). The design is paired (tasks are the pairing unit); for each task we generate exactly one shared initial candidate configuration using the declared prompt and model snapshot. Baseline outcome = validator(initial) (no further model calls); guarded outcome = validator(initial) or, if the initial candidate fails, a single automatic repair generation is attempted and the repaired candidate revalidated. The per‑task binary outcome is success if the arm produced a validator‑pass within the arm’s call budget (baseline ≤1 call; guarded ≤2). The experiment fixed seeds for metadata determinism; stopping rule: run all 300 tasks once.

Task manifest and validator. We used a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest restricted to vendor CLI fragments expressing concrete configuration‑change intents (Cisco IOS / JunOS / Arista fragments represented). Each manifest entry encodes intent, required safe sequence constraints, an initial network state, and an expected final state. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) performs: CLI parsing and canonicalization; syntactic checks; interface assignment and existence invariants; workflow constraints (e.g., required down‑before‑change, make‑before‑break patterns); and destructive‑pattern detection. The validator outputs canonicalized final configurations, a boolean pass/fail verdict, and structured diagnostic traces (violation codes, touched fields, parsed command counts). All validator traces are archived per episode under execution/scoring/*. Representative scoring artifacts are execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d0...).

Model and prompting. The declared generator snapshot was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 above). For reproducibility we archived the exact model call traces (execution/provider_calls/) and raw responses (execution/responses/). The preregistration constrained the generator to a single shared initial call per task; repair prompts and templates were frozen and archived; repair generation was allowed only under the guarded policy and only once per task.

Statistical analysis. The primary pre‑specified test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired 2×2 contingency table (n11,n10,n01,n00) plus a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729 (both preregistered). Secondary pre‑specified analyses included per‑vendor paired tests with Bonferroni correction (family alpha = 0.05 → per‑comparison alpha ≈ 0.0167). Analysis code and inputs/outputs are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0).
sections.results:
Execution bookkeeping and artifact verification. The run executed exactly the preregistered contract: planned episodes = 600 (300 tasks × 2 arms using a shared initial); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Model calls used = 300 (one shared initial generation per task; no repair calls were consumed because none were required). All raw outputs, provider traces, scoring artifacts, and hashes are archived; execution manifest lists every artifact and SHA‑256 hash (execution/execution_manifest.json). Representative artifacts: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = 1acce92558ed...), execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...), execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb...).

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). Every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator without repair: baseline_success_count = 300/300; guarded_success_count = 300/300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 above). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because n10 = n01 = 0 there were no discordant pairs; the preregistered single‑repair policy was not invoked on any task and repair_call_count = 0.

Per‑vendor preregistered secondary tests. The preregistration pre‑specified per‑vendor paired comparisons. We executed the confirmatory analysis exactly as specified and observed zero discordant pairs overall and therefore within every vendor subgroup; in that situation per‑vendor paired McNemar tests cannot produce informative p‑values because the contingency tables for each subgroup also contain zero discordance. We therefore report transparently that the preregistered per‑vendor paired tests were not informative due to absence of discordant pairs. The authoritative task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3) contains vendor labels for each task and is archived for auditors that wish to compute vendor counts or to rerun subgrouped designs under alternative generator or prompt choices.

Representative episode diagnostics. Scorer traces show validator diagnostics (parsed command counts, touched fields, final canonicalized configuration, and violation codes). Example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json records parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validator verdict valid = true, and the canonicalized final_configuration. For three representative tasks (task‑000001..000003) the shared initial, baseline, and guarded responses are identical and passed the validator (artifact paths and SHA‑256 values are listed in the artifact bundle).
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation. The confirmatory design isolates the incremental value of a bounded single repair on the very same generator output by using a shared initial candidate per task. That design reduces confounding from generator variability but also reduces sensitivity when the generator is already highly accurate on the chosen task distribution. In our run the generator+prompt+model snapshot produced a ceiling outcome: every shared initial candidate satisfied the conservative deterministic validator. Under that observed ceiling, the guarded policy could not increase validator pass probability because there were no initial failures to repair; the paired difference is therefore exactly 0.00 and the bootstrap CI collapses to a point.

This artifact‑grounded outcome does not imply repairs are never useful. It implies that, for the supplied manifest, model snapshot, and prompt, validator failures were absent. The practical message is narrower and actionable: when the generator produces validator‑passing outputs on a task distribution, adding a bounded automatic repair stage (and its runtime costs) will not increase deterministic pass rates. Whether repairs help in other regimes depends on generator error rate and task hardness.

Why the ceiling occurred. Possible contributors (all testable via replays): (1) task manifest difficulty relative to the generator snapshot; (2) prompt formulation and few‑shot scaffolding used for the generator; (3) the particular model snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) and its alignment tuning. Because we archived provider traces, raw responses, and the manifest, exact replay and controlled scans (increase adversariality, change prompt, allow independent initial draws per arm, or permit iterative repair) are straightforward reproducibility steps. All those follow‑ups are outside the confirmatory run but can be driven from the archived artifacts without changing the study provenance.

Per‑vendor analysis note. The preregistered per‑vendor secondary paired tests were not informative because there were no discordant pairs overall; therefore subgroup contingency tables also had zero discordance. Auditors can retrieve the vendor distribution from the canonical task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 above) and replay alternative generator prompts or snapshots to create the discordance necessary to measure repair value across vendors.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variability but trades sensitivity to ceiling effects. Execution determinism is supported by archived seeds and provider traces. Construct validity: our deterministic validator measures a conservative set of operational invariants (syntactic correctness, interface and workflow constraints); it deliberately omits dynamic emulation or live routing semantics and therefore may under‑approximate some safety failures. External validity: a single model snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) and a curated 300‑task manifest limit generalizability; different models, prompts, or adversarial task banks can change outcomes. Conclusion validity: because discordance = 0 the paired test cannot detect improvements; the statistical result is an accurate reflection of observed data and not a failure of the test procedure.

Practical implications. Operators and system designers should not assume every G‑V‑R pipeline will measurably improve deterministic pass rates. Instead, empirical evaluation should target the operational regime where initial generator errors occur: increase task difficulty, use independent initial draws per arm, or evaluate repair under broader budgets. Our artifact bundle enables such targeted follow‑ups and exact reproduction of the null‑discordance regime we observed.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment isolating the marginal effect of a bounded single automatic repair on LLM‑produced vendor CLI candidates. For the supplied 300‑task manifest, prompt, and gpt‑5‑mini snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the conservative deterministic validator, so the preregistered single‑repair step was not invoked and produced no measurable benefit (paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]). This artifact‑grounded null outcome indicates that G‑V‑R's marginal benefit depends on the generator error rate for the target intent distribution. We provide the full archived preregistration, manifest, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts with canonical SHA‑256 hashes to enable exact reproduction and controlled follow‑ups that vary task hardness, generator prompt, model snapshot, or repair budget.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface and workflow invariants) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; under the chosen prompt and model snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the validator (ceiling effect), limiting the ability to measure G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered one‑repair policy.

Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this reduces sensitivity to generator variability and can mask repair value when the generator is already accurate on the task set.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not evaluated.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary reported zero flagged pairs but residual uncertainty remains.
